topics.title: 40.1 Pipes
topics.summary: pipe returns two descriptors: one for reading and one for writing. Bytes written to the write end become available at the read end in order. The pipe does not preserve arbitrary application message boundaries as a record protocol. A reader sees end of file only after all write-end references are closed and buffered bytes have been consumed. “The original writer exited” is insufficient when another process accidentally retains a write descriptor.

topics.title: 40.2 Pipe buffers
topics.summary: The kernel stores a bounded amount of pending pipe data. Buffer capacity is not the same as PIPE_BUF , which concerns atomicity guarantees for appropriately sized writes under the documented conditions. Large writes from several writers can interleave. A multiwriter protocol must define record sizes and synchronization rather than assume that one source-level write always becomes one indivisible record. Capacity can vary with system configuration and policy.

topics.title: 40.3 Blocking
topics.summary: A blocking read waits when the pipe is empty but writers still exist. A blocking write can wait when capacity is unavailable. If all read ends are closed, writing can cause SIGPIPE or report EPIPE when signal policy permits the error to be observed. These rules make lifecycle mistakes visible as hangs or unexpected termination. Waiting for a producer before starting its consumer can deadlock when the producer fills the pipe. Start communicating participants before waiting for their completion.

topics.title: 40.4 File-descriptor duplication
topics.summary: Duplication creates another descriptor referring to the same open file description. Both descriptors keep the underlying open object referenced until each is closed. The new descriptor is a new ownership obligation even though it refers to the same object. Duplication shares the underlying offset and status where applicable; it does not copy file contents or create an independent seek position. Descriptor-specific flags have separate rules and should be set deliberately.

topics.summary: dup chooses an available descriptor number and makes it refer to the same open file description as the source. It is useful when preserving an existing stream before temporary redirection. The copied integer value alone would not preserve anything: closing the original table entry would invalidate all variables holding that number. dup creates an actual additional kernel reference.

topics.title: 40.6 dup2
topics.summary: dup2(oldfd, newfd) makes a specific descriptor number refer to the source object, atomically replacing an existing target reference when appropriate. This avoids the race in a separate close(newfd) followed by dup(oldfd) sequence. When oldfd == newfd and the descriptor is valid, the operation leaves it as that descriptor. Cleanup code must not then blindly close the source number if doing so would close the newly intended standard stream. The example below tests this case before closing the source reference.

topics.title: 40.9 Pipelines
topics.summary: A pipeline connects several processes so that one process’s output feeds the next process’s input. The parent creates pipes, launches all stages, closes its unused ends, and then waits according to its policy. Every child must close pipe ends it does not need. In a longer pipeline, this includes descriptors for other stages, not only its immediate neighbor. A descriptor ownership table is often the clearest way to design and review the launch sequence.
